builder_plan.scenario: An agent reads external documents or tool responses that may contain malicious instructions.
builder_plan.change: Replay attacks and legitimate lookalikes in an isolated copy of your agent workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your existing checks with the same tasks, permissions, and tool responses.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful attacks missed, legitimate actions blocked, detection delay, and review cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: CASEL: Consequence-Aware Selective Execution for Reliable Long-Horizon Tool-Using Agents
summary: It replaces generic uncertainty-threshold gating of tool calls with a per-call cost-minimizing allocation across execute, verify, sandbox, clarify, approve, and abstain, using calibrated failure probability, consequence, reversibility, ambiguity, and evidence freshness. The cost is engineering complexity: per-call state and consequence estimation, calibration infrastructure, sandboxing and approval plumbing, and added latency on routed calls, though no extra model compute. Results are simulator-only under assumed intervention effectiveness, so real-world benefit is unvalidated; miscalibrated consequence or failure estimates could misroute calls, and the human-approval load may be operationally heavy for a small team.
rationale: The method is a runtime policy compatible with API-based models, but its gains are demonstrated only in a controlled simulation with assumed intervention effectiveness, so a constrained team should track it rather than adopt before independent validation.
technique: Consequence-aware selective execution for tool-using agents

claims.statement: It replaces generic uncertainty-threshold gating of tool calls with a per-call cost-minimizing allocation across execute, verify, sandbox, clarify, approve, and abstain, using calibrated failure probability, consequence, reversibility, ambiguity, and evidence freshness. The cost is engineering complexity: per-call state and consequence estimation, calibration infrastructure, sandboxing and approval plumbing, and added latency on routed calls, though no extra model compute. Results are simulator-only under assumed intervention effectiveness, so real-world benefit is unvalidated; miscalibrated consequence or failure estimates could misroute calls, and the human-approval load may be operationally heavy for a small team.

In simulation, CASEL reduces harmful-side-effect trajectories from 14.75% (uncertainty-ranked gate) to 7.02% and mean normalized harm from 0.184 to 0.123; a failure-probability-times-consequence gate reaches similar harm but with 45% more human approvals.
